Sharing your work

Exporting notes

Because Clew's reading mode is the jmarkdown typesetting engine — a dual-output engine that compiles the same source to HTML and to LaTeX — exporting is not an afterthought bolted onto a preview. Any note exports to a standalone HTML page, to print-quality LaTeX source, or, when a TeX toolchain is installed, straight to a typeset PDF. The mathematics, theorem environments, citations, and diagrams you see in reading mode survive into print, because print was always one of the engine's two native targets.

Where the commands live

The export commands for the current note sit under File → Export:

  • As HTML…
  • As LaTeX…
  • As PDF (via LaTeX)…
  • As PDF (reading view)…

(The last item in that submenu, Vault as Website…, exports the whole vault at once and has its own chapter; in a note that belongs to a book, Book as PDF (via LaTeX), Book as LaTeX, Book as HTML and Book as PDF (reading view) build the whole book, and in a chapter Proof This Chapter (PDF via LaTeX) typesets that chapter alone, numbered as in the book — not in 0.12.0.) The same four commands are in the command palette (⌘P) as Export note as HTML, Export note as LaTeX (.tex), Export note as PDF (via LaTeX) and Export note as PDF (reading view), and like every command they can be given hotkeys in the hotkey editor. All four act on the active note's tab and need a note to be open. From a terminal, clew export --html|--latex|--pdf <note> runs the first three on a note you name, writing just the one file beside it or where --out says; see Links and the command line. (Not in 0.12.0.)

Each command opens a save dialog. The suggested destination is the vault root, with the note's own name and the right extension (.html, .tex, or .pdf); you can point it anywhere on disk. Nothing is written until you confirm the dialog, and cancelling it cancels the export.

On iPad Clew for iOS has two of the four, in the command palette: Export note as HTML and Export note as PDF (reading view). The LaTeX export and the PDF via LaTeX need a TeX installation and stay on the desktop. There is no save dialog on the iPad: the exported file is offered in the share sheet, so Save to Files puts it anywhere Files can reach — the vault included — and Print, Markup and AirDrop are a tap away. The reading-view PDF is made on the device from the same rendered page, figures and mathematics included, at the paper size in Settings.

One source, three outputs

The point of exporting through the engine — rather than only printing the preview to PDF, as most note apps do — is that each of these formats is generated natively from the Markdown source:

  • HTML produces a complete, standalone web page using the engine's own page templates. Mathematics is typeset, citations are resolved against your bibliography, diagrams render, footnotes and cross-references link up. It is a document you can mail to someone or drop on a server as-is.
  • LaTeX produces real LaTeX source: theorem environments become \begin{theorem}, displayed equations keep their AMS numbering, citations go through natbib, figures become floats, and TikZ pictures are emitted as native TikZ — not as embedded screenshots. The .tex file is yours to edit, include in a larger document, or hand to a journal. By default it is set in Clew's style: EB Garamond, 12pt, A4.
  • PDF is the LaTeX route carried one step further: Clew generates the .tex and then runs your TeX toolchain on it. The result is a typeset page in the full LaTeX sense — proper line breaking, real fonts, print-ready mathematics.

Callouts come through both. The HTML draws them as reading mode does — your own types included, a foldable one still folding — and the LaTeX makes each a coloured tcolorbox with the same icon and title, printed open; a long one breaks across pages with its strip and tint on every page. (In 0.12.0 a note's export draws only GitHub's upper-case alerts, > [!NOTE] to > [!CAUTION], as boxes — without a custom title or folding — and every other callout comes out as an ordinary quote with its [!type] written out.)

In 0.12.0 A LaTeX export in 0.12.0 does not load the natbib package its citations need. As PDF via LaTeX, a note that cites prints each citation as its bare key — lewis1969 — with no reference list, and the .tex does not compile as it stands. Export such a note as PDF (reading view), or export the LaTeX and load natbib in its preamble yourself (\usepackage{natbib}; for \fullcite, bibentry too). And TeX meets an error, though the PDF is still made, in a note with an & or # in a list item (or in a theorem inside one) or with a Mermaid or MetaPost figure. The & or # is lost, with a line break in its place, and every piece of code in the PDF, inline or a block, prints as <MINTED>. PDF (reading view) is the way round this too.

Diagrams go in a folder beside the file

Some diagrams an export draws itself rather than passing their source through: a MetaPost figure or a native Mermaid diagram in LaTeX, the TeX figures in HTML. It keeps what it draws in a cache of Clew's own, outside the vault, and copies the figures each file uses into a folder beside that file, named after it — Report.tex or Report.html gets Report-figures/, with a folder inside for each kind (mermaid/, MetaPost/, TiKZ/) — and refers to them there by a relative path. A kept .tex or .html therefore stands on its own: move it or send it with its folder and every figure is still found. A note's .tex and .html share the one folder; a book's go into build/ (Building a book).

The folder is the export's, and safe to delete: the next export makes it again. Before exporting, Clew moves the folder it made last time to the Trash, so a diagram since taken out of the note leaves no copy behind — unless the note's other export still uses it (a .html beside the .tex), when it is kept. Clew marks the folders it makes and never touches one it did not: if a folder of yours already has that name, the figures are not copied into it, and the export's warnings say so and what to do — rename or move your folder, then export again. Until you do, the file refers to Clew's cache on this computer, which is pruned, so it will not travel (from a restricted vault, to a temporary folder already removed, so its diagrams do not show).

The cache is in Clew's own data folder, and later exports of the same vault reuse it; every vault's together is kept under 500 MB, the figures used least recently going first. A vault you have not trusted keeps no cache at all: each export draws into a temporary folder that is removed when it ends. Either way an export writes nothing into the vault but the file you asked for and its figures folder. Folders such as mermaid/, MetaPost/ or TiKZ/ that an earlier version's exports left beside your notes are yours now; Clew does not touch them. (In 0.12.0 an export keeps its figures in those folders, beside the note, and the file it writes refers to them there.)

Two PDFs, for two different wishes

As PDF (reading view) is the other thing people mean by "export to PDF": not a typeset paper, but this, on paper — the note exactly as the reading pane draws it, callout colours, syntax highlighting, mermaid diagrams, editable-looking tables and all. Clew prints the very same rendered page the app shows you.

Pick between them by what you want the document to be. The LaTeX PDF is for a paper, a handout, anything whose typography should be the argument's equal — and it needs a TeX toolchain. The reading-view PDF needs nothing installed, takes a second, and looks like Clew: right for circulating lecture notes, sending a colleague what is on your screen, or keeping a copy of a note as you had it.

Three details are worth knowing. It prints in the light theme whatever the app is wearing, because the engine's own styling is written for a light page and a PDF is a paper artifact. Paper size comes from Settings → Appearance → PDF paper size (A4 by default; US Letter, Legal and Tabloid are there too). And a folded embed prints folded — "as displayed" is the promise, so if you want an embed's contents in the PDF, unfold it first.

This is the practical payoff of the design commitment described in the introduction: a note about, say, a convergence proof — with numbered equations, a theorem, a couple of citations from your .bib file — renders in the app, exports as a web page, and typesets as a paper, all from the file you were editing a minute ago. Nothing needs to be rewritten for print.

Exports use your jmarkdown configuration

Here is the subtle point of this chapter, and it is worth understanding because it explains everything else about how exports behave. When Clew renders a note for reading mode, it runs the engine with a private configuration of its own — one that loads Clew's wikilink and fence extensions, points at local assets, and uses Clew's preview template. When Clew exports a note, it deliberately does not use that configuration. Instead, the export runs the engine in a fresh process whose working directory is the note's own folder, which means the engine's normal configuration cascade applies: the built-in defaults, then your global ~/.jmarkdown configuration, then any .jmarkdown/ folder next to the note.

In other words, an export behaves exactly as if you had run the jmarkdown command-line tool on the file yourself (a LaTeX export adds Clew's style, below). That is a feature:

  • Exports use the engine's own page and LaTeX templates — including any customisations you have made to them — rather than Clew's app-oriented preview template.
  • Your bibliography setup, citation style, and other engine options from ~/.jmarkdown are honoured. One vault setting reaches an export as well: the vault's bibliography (Settings → This vault), used alongside any the note names itself — see A vault-wide bibliography (not in 0.12.0, where an export reads only the note's own).
  • Power users can keep a .jmarkdown/ configuration folder next to a set of notes to control precisely how those notes export — different templates for different projects, extra engine extensions, LaTeX preamble additions — without touching how the notes look inside Clew.
  • A note's own metadata header still applies, as it does in the preview.

One per-vault setting does carry over: if the vault is set to standard Markdown syntax (the normal syntax toggle in Settings → This vault, described in the dialect chapter), exports honour it, so a vault written in ordinary Markdown exports as ordinary Markdown.

And one exception runs the other way: a vault this device has not trusted exports without running its notes' code, and from your global ~/.jmarkdown alone — a .jmarkdown/ folder inside the vault is not read, since it too could carry code. It makes no PDF via LaTeX at all, which would run your TeX installation over the vault's own TeX: that is refused by name, before anything is built, and the notice offers the reading-view PDF, or trusting the vault, instead (Troubleshooting; not in 0.12.0).

Caution — Clew's preview extensions do not apply Clew's Obsidian-flavoured additions are extensions loaded by the preview configuration, and single-note exports do not load them; the engine's own Obsidian links stand in for two. Concretely: an inline [[wikilink]] prints as its text, not as a link — the alias if it has one, else the note's name, or Note > Heading for a link to a heading. An ![[image]] embed is included, the image found anywhere in the vault as in reading mode, at the size a |300 or |300x200 after its name asks for; the HTML or LaTeX refers to it where it lies, by a path relative to the exported file, never by its full path on your disk. A note cannot be embedded: ![[Note]] prints as its name, with a warning. (In 0.12.0 all three come out as written.) The ```mermaid, ```leaflet and ```query fences render as plain code blocks (see Troubleshooting). Tabbing is the engine's own and exports whole. (In 0.12.0 a ```tabbing fence is a code block too, which a PDF via LaTeX prints as <MINTED>, and a @begin(tabbing) environment loses its tab commands.) The engine's native forms still work — :::mermaid or @begin(mermaid) blocks export fine, in LaTeX and PDF as figures (Diagrams in export), and everything in math, citations, and the engine's own diagram machinery is native. A note you intend to publish as a paper is best written leaning on the engine's own vocabulary; a note leaning on Clew's vault features is better shared via website export, which does load all of Clew's extensions.
Caution — own-line wikilinks become inclusions The engine has its own meaning for a [[chapter.md]] standing alone on a line: file inclusion, and it is on by default in the engine's configuration. In an export, such a line splices the named file's contents into the document — useful on purpose for book-style projects (it is the same behaviour the per-vault jmarkdown project setting brings into the preview), but surprising if you meant it as a mere link. Add File inclusion: false to a note's metadata header or a .jmarkdown/ config next to the note to switch it off.

Clew's style for LaTeX

A LaTeX export and a PDF via LaTeX — a note's or a book's — come out in Clew's style: EB Garamond, with Garamond-Math for the mathematics, at 12pt on A4; microtype; curly quotes from straight ones; hyphenation in the note's language; quieter lists and headings, and long quotations a size smaller; emoji in colour; and links without boxes round them. The language is the Lang in the note's header, else the one your jmarkdown configuration sets, else English; and English, a bare en included, is your region's — British, American, Canadian and so on. A language babel does not know (ja, say) gets no hyphenation from the style, and where babel or polyglossia is loaded already — by your configuration's preamble, or by a book whose chapters are in other languages (What a chapter may set for itself) — the style leaves the hyphenation to it. The paper is US Letter where the region uses it — the United States, Canada, Mexico and a few others — and A4 elsewhere. The region is the one in that Lang (en-US, say), or else your computer's.

The style is added to your jmarkdown configuration, not put in its place: your configuration's packages and preamble still load, and a layout it sets — Class options, Geometry — is kept, the style setting one only where neither your configuration nor the note's header does. Class options that name no paper (11pt) still get the region's paper, which the style then sets through its geometry — unless a Geometry is set as well, which must name the paper itself. The fonts are the exception: EB Garamond replaces a main font your configuration sets with \setmainfont. A note's own header wins over both, as it wins over any configuration: a key it sets — Class options, Geometry, Packages, LaTeX preamble — replaces the style's and your configuration's whole, so a header's LaTeX preamble takes the style's fonts and hyphenation with it and leaves LaTeX's default face.

The style needs the EB Garamond and Garamond-Math fonts. MacTeX and a full TeX Live have both; BasicTeX does not, and tlmgr install ebgaramond garamond-math adds them. Without them the document keeps LaTeX's default face and still compiles. It needs LuaLaTeX or XeLaTeX too — Automatic compiles it with LuaLaTeX (Which TeX engine), the one engine that draws its emoji in colour — so with pdfLaTeX chosen in Settings, or a note's header saying LaTeX engine: pdflatex, the style is left out altogether.

Settings → Appearance → Style of LaTeX and PDF via LaTeX exports turns it off. Your jmarkdown configuration only (latexExportStyle: none; the default, Clew (EB Garamond), is clew) exports from your configuration alone, as before — with nothing configured, LaTeX's own defaults: Computer Modern at 10pt on US Letter, quotation marks as typed. (Not in 0.12.0, whose exports are always your configuration alone.)

PDF export and the TeX toolchain

PDF export needs a TeX installation on your machine — Clew does not bundle one, because a TeX distribution is enormous and you likely already have one if you want this feature. On macOS, MacTeX is the usual choice. Clew looks for latexmk first, in the standard installation directories (/Library/TeX/texbin, /usr/local/bin, and /opt/homebrew/bin). With it, reruns for cross-references and bibliographies are handled automatically, which is why it is preferred; without it, Clew runs the TeX engine itself. latexmk reads only its system-wide configuration and yours — ~/.latexmkrc, or ~/.config/latexmk/latexmkrc — and the biber it runs only yours (~/.biber.conf, ~/.config/biber/biber.conf, or on a Mac ~/Library/biber/biber.conf): a latexmkrc or biber.conf in a note's or a book's folder, its build/ included, or where you save the PDF, is never read. (In 0.12.0, which compiles where you save the PDF, latexmk reads a latexmkrc there too.)

Which TeX engine

Clew also chooses the engine. Left on Automatic, it reads the generated .tex: a document that loads fontspec, unicode-math or polyglossia, or runs Lua code — a \setmainfont in your jmarkdown configuration's LaTeX preamble, say — is compiled with LuaLaTeX; one that needs a XeTeX-only package such as xeCJK, with XeLaTeX; anything else with pdfLaTeX. Clew's style loads unicode-math, so a document in it is compiled with LuaLaTeX. Reading the document catches whatever put the package there — your configuration, the vault's, the note's own header. For what it cannot see, Settings → Appearance → LaTeX engine (PDF via LaTeX export) names one engine for every export. (Not in 0.12.0, which always runs pdfLaTeX, so a preamble that loads fontspec stops every PDF via LaTeX.)

A related detail that saves real head-scratching: apps launched from the Dock or Finder inherit a minimal PATH that usually lacks the TeX directories, which is why "it works in my terminal but not in the app" is such a common failure elsewhere. Clew sidesteps it by extending the PATH it hands to every engine process with the common TeX and Homebrew locations (/Library/TeX/texbin, /opt/homebrew/bin, /usr/local/bin). This matters for anything that shells out to a TeX program by name: the latex run behind this export, and your TeX's figure tools when an export sends a figure to them. (TikZ and MetaPost figures need none of it, in the preview or, by default, in an export: those engines ship with Clew, as WebAssembly — see Who draws an export's figures.) On Windows, TeX installers put themselves on the PATH, so no extension is needed.

Mechanically, a PDF export writes the intermediate .tex into a temporary folder and compiles it there, with the note's own folder on TeX's search paths, so the note's images and its .bib are found wherever you save the PDF. Then it delivers the PDF alone and removes the folder: no .tex, .aux, .log or figures land beside the PDF. (In 0.12.0 the .tex is written next to the PDF and compiled there, and it stays, with LaTeX's own files.) The compiler runs in nonstop mode with a three-minute timeout (two in 0.12.0). One pragmatic wrinkle: a TeX engine can exit with a non-zero status on mere warnings, so Clew accepts the run whenever it wrote the PDF — that run: a PDF an earlier export left at the same path does not count (in 0.12.0 it did, and could hide a failure). When there is none, the error says which engine ran, why it was chosen, and the first error in the compiler's log.

Tip — the .tex file is your debugging window A PDF export keeps nothing but the PDF, so to see the LaTeX behind it, export the note as LaTeX: the same .tex, with its figures in the folder beside it. If a compile fails or the output looks wrong, run latexmk on that .tex yourself, with -pdf, -lualatex or -xelatex for the engine the export used: you get the full compiler output, and you can fix or restyle the LaTeX directly. Exporting to LaTeX first and compiling by hand is exactly the same pipeline, one step at a time. (In 0.12.0 the PDF export leaves its .tex, and LaTeX's .log and auxiliary files, beside the PDF.)

Troubleshooting

"A PDF via LaTeX is not made in a vault this Mac does not trust"
The vault is restricted on this device, and Clew makes no PDF via LaTeX there. The notice reads in full: A PDF via LaTeX is not made in a vault this Mac does not trust: it would run your TeX installation over the vault's own TeX, which can read any file you can. Export the note as PDF (reading view), or trust the vault (Settings → This vault). On Windows and Linux it says this computer. Nothing is built, and Clew does not ask where to save. Export the note as PDF (reading view), which needs no TeX, or trust the vault in Settings → This vault and export again. clew export --pdf prints the same words and exits with 1; a book's PDF is refused in the same way. (Not in 0.12.0.)
"No TeX toolchain found"
Clew could not find latexmk, or the engine it chose (the message names both), in any of the directories listed above. Install MacTeX (or your platform's TeX distribution) and try again; no restart of Clew should be needed if the tools land in one of the standard locations.
The PDF was not produced
The LaTeX compile failed hard enough that no PDF appeared. The message names the engine that ran, why it was chosen, and the first error in the compiler's log — often enough on its own. A Fatal Package fontspec Error under pdfLaTeX means the document needs a Unicode engine that Automatic could not see (a package of your own that loads fontspec, say) or that Settings names pdfLaTeX: choose LuaLaTeX there. Otherwise export the same note as LaTeX and compile it in a terminal — the compiler's error messages will name the offending line. Common causes are a missing LaTeX package and raw HTML in the note, which has no LaTeX equivalent.
The PDF via LaTeX is not in EB Garamond
Clew's style was left out, or could not find its fonts. Settings → Appearance may say Your jmarkdown configuration only for the style, or name pdfLaTeX as the LaTeX engine; a note whose header says LaTeX engine: pdflatex gets no style, and one whose header sets LaTeX preamble replaces the style's fonts with its own lines. Or the TeX installation lacks EB Garamond and Garamond-Math: BasicTeX does, and tlmgr install ebgaramond garamond-math adds them. (Not in 0.12.0, which has no style.)
A Clew fence prints as its source in PDF via LaTeX
A LaTeX export sets each fenced block as a minted listing named after its language. The Pygments highlighter behind minted knows none of Clew's own fence languages — ```query, ```mermaid, ```kanban, ```dataview and the like — so such a block is set as plain text: the PDF shows the fence's source, not the table or diagram, and the export warns once for each such language. For what reading mode shows, export the note as PDF (reading view), which prints it fences and all (see Two PDFs), or as a website. (In 0.12.0 the PDF is made without a warning, and each such block prints as <MINTED>: minted could not set it, and only the compiler's log says why — Pygments lexer … is unknown.)
The export's notice lists warnings
The engine checks every note for what would trouble LaTeX, and an export that found any says so — LaTeX export: dollars, braces. Whatever else the export reported, such as a diagram left out or a note embed printed as its name, is counted at the end (· 1 other), and the ⚠ lists each one in full. The same warnings show as a ⚠ in the status bar while you write; see The status bar for what each kind means and how to silence one. (Not in 0.12.0.)
Citations show as question marks in the PDF
The bibliography did not resolve. Check that the note's bibliography setup (see Citations and bibliographies) points at a .bib file the export can reach from the note's own folder — exports run from the note's directory, not from wherever Clew was started, and wherever you save the PDF, that folder is where its .bib is looked for.
The export looks different from reading mode
Almost always the configuration-cascade point above: the preview runs with Clew's extensions and per-vault settings, the export runs with yours. Obsidian-style fences and query blocks are the usual suspects, and wikilinks, which print as their text.
The exported HTML page needs the network
Unlike Clew's preview, which uses only local assets, the engine's own HTML template may reference assets such as MathJax from a CDN. The page is standalone in the sense of being a single file, but rendering mathematics in the browser can require a network connection, depending on your jmarkdown template configuration.
Obsidian compatibility Obsidian's PDF export prints its HTML preview to a PDF — a picture of the app's rendering. Clew's PDF export generates LaTeX and typesets it, which is a different kind of artifact: selectable, searchable, journal-grade output with real mathematics. The trade is the one this chapter describes — the export pipeline speaks jmarkdown, not Obsidian's dialect, so it shines brightest on notes written with the engine's own vocabulary.

LaTeX File → Export → As LaTeX… Export note as LaTeX (.tex) A .tex source file; relative graphics resolve from where it is saved. The diagrams the export draws go into a -figures/ folder beside it (not in 0.12.0). Nothing extra (a TeX installation to compile it later).
